newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Kidnappers seize UN workers in Tajik capital.
newsitem.headline: Kidnappers seize UN workers in Tajik capital.

text.p: Four United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) workers were seized in the Tajikistan capital Dushanbe on Thursday, the latest victims of a spate of kidnappings to hit the chronically unstable republic.
The identities of the kidnappers were not known.

In Geneva, a UNHCR spokeswoman, Hedayat Abdel Nabi, said the agency had had no contact with the four -- a UNHCR expatriate from Nigeria, a Tajik security guard and two Tajik drivers -- since they went missing in the centre of capital Dushanbe on Thursday morning with two marked U.N. cars.

She said UNHCR had no independent field information, but U.N. observers based in Tajikistan had reported that the four were captured on Thursday by the same armed Tajik rebel group which seized four U.N. military observers from Austria, Switzerland and Ukraine, two Red Cross workers and four Russian journalists.

The U.N. observers said the four had been taken to a place called Obigarm in the central Garm valley and some 80 km (50 miles) from Dushanbe in the remote, mountainous Central Asian republic, Abdel Nabi said.

"U.N. observers in Tajikistan informed us that they are being held together with the other hostages. But we don't know anything about the details of this incident and we've had no contact with the kidnappers," she said.
It was the first time UNHCR staff were kidnapped in the former Soviet Central Asia, she added.

The latest hostage taking was a set-back for embattled Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov who on Thursday pledged to win the freedom of the journalists and U.N. military observers taken earlier this week.

Russia's foreign ministry said Moscow would use all its resources, including special services, to free journalists seized this week. Itar-Tass news agency said it had received a telephone call from a kidnapped reporter saying she was well.
The rebels are commanded by Rizvon Sadirov, who used to fight for Tajikistan's Islamic opposition but whose loyalties are now unclear.

The rebels want safe passage for members of the group based in neighbouring Afghanistan back into the former Soviet republic, an impoverished, mountainous country wracked by civil war which also borders China.
"The president held an urgent meeting of the government this morning," presidential spokesman Zafar Saidov said. "He gave them the task of freeing hostages today by peaceful means."
Saidov said Rakhmonov had ordered General Gafar Mirzoyev, head of his presidential guard, to start negotiations with the rebels, who are led by Rizvon Sadirov.

"Mirzoyev has already left for the area controlled by Sadirov's men to start talks on the release of hostages," Saidov said. "The president told the government meeting that there is no threat to the life of the hostages at the moment."
Russian First Deputy Foreign Miniser Boris Pastukhov told Interfax News Agency Moscow would do everything necessary to free Russian hostages. He called the kidnappings banditry.
"We will use all channels, including special services and contacts with Afghan field commanders," he said.

Itar_Tass said it had received a telephone call from one of its correspondents held by the kidnappers. It said she told them that all was well and they should not worry. There were no further details.
The United States embassy in Dushanbe urged all foreigners in the republic to exercise extreme caution.

"Everyone should exercise extreme caution, especially when travelling home," William Davnie, deputy chief of the U.S. mission in Dushanbe, told Reuters by telephone. "We have also recommended against any unnecessary travel," he said.
The U.N. and the International Committee of the Red Cross have condemned the kidnappings and have demanded the hostages' immediate release.
Local staff at both agencies have been told to stay at home until Monday.
Foreign diplomats in the Tajik capital Dushanbe say that Rakhmonov controls only 15 to 20 percent of Tajik territory.

Tens of thousands of people were killed and many more made homeless during a four-year civil war in Tajikistan. But a ceasefire agreed between the government and the guerrillas has held for nearly two months and further peace talks are due to be held on February 26 in Moscow.
Last December, Sadyrov's group took 23 people hostage, including seven U.N. observers, to demand the release of his brother. All the hostages were later released.
